# Use-Case Fit

## Goal-to-Tool Mapping

| Goal | Best Tool(s) | Why |
|------|-------------|-----|
| Codebase comprehension | pyan3 [15], PyCG + pyvis | Static graph of define/use relationships |
| Performance profiling | py-spy [21], gprof2dot [24] | Flamegraphs with minimal overhead |
| Dead code detection | Vulture [30] | Confidence-scored unused code |
| Security taint analysis | Pysa [47], Semgrep Pro [49] | Interprocedural data flow tracking |
| Vulnerability reachability | Snyk [52], Endor Labs [51] | Call graph-based CVE prioritization |
| Refactoring impact analysis | PyCG [1], pyan3 [15] | Which functions are affected by changes |
| Dependency cycle detection | pydeps [27], importlab [28] | Module-level import graph analysis |
| Runtime debugging | VizTracer [31], Hunter [22] | Interactive execution tracing |
| Documentation | Jonga [35], pyan3 [15] | Sphinx integration, SVG/HTML output |
| Async call tracing | Python 3.14 asyncio [40] | Structured awaiter graph capture |

## Codebase Comprehension

Call graphs help visualize code structure "when taking over or maintaining a
Python project" [10]. They provide "a high-level overview of how everything
fits together" [10]. Call graph multilevel hierarchical abstractions assist
developers in understanding "from high-level abstraction to low-level
implementation" [10].

Practical application: generating a call graph to identify which functions to
group when splitting large files during refactoring [10]. Spaghetti code
becomes "visible from the call graph" where methods calling each other make
it "hard to figure out who called who" [10].

**Tool recommendation:** pyan3 in `--module-level` mode for high-level view
[15], switching to function-level for specific modules of interest.

## Performance Profiling

Flamegraphs consistently outperform call graphs for identifying performance
bottlenecks [8]. Call graphs show static potential ("what could happen");
flamegraphs show actual behavior ("what did happen") with relative time [8].

**Tool recommendation:** py-spy for production (~1% overhead) [21], cProfile +
gprof2dot for development (3.2% overhead) [24][38]. Do not use sys.settrace-
based tools for performance — 10x+ overhead distorts the measurements [59].

## Dead Code Detection

Vulture finds unused classes, functions, and variables via AST analysis with
confidence scores from 60% to 100% [30]. False positive rate is high for
dynamic code — 59 false positives reported on a codebase with zero real issues
[66]. Whitelist files are the standard mitigation [30].

Dead code detection in Python is undecidable [56]. Frameworks (Django, Flask)
with dynamic dispatch, string-based imports, and plugin systems make false
positives inevitable [56].

**Tool recommendation:** Vulture with `--min-confidence 100` for high-certainty
findings [30]. For frameworks, maintain a whitelist and accept that some dead
code will be missed.

## Security Analysis

See [security-taint-analysis.md](security-taint-analysis.md) for detailed
coverage. Summary:

- **Simple projects:** Bandit (AST pattern matching, zero setup) [47]
- **Medium projects:** Semgrep CE (intraprocedural taint, rule registry) [49]
- **Enterprise/large projects:** Pysa or CodeQL (interprocedural, cross-file)
  [47][49]

## When NOT to Use Call Graph Tools

1. **Small scripts (<500 LoC):** IDE "Find All References" is faster and
   sufficient. Call graph tools add setup overhead for minimal value.
2. **Framework-heavy code (Django, Flask):** Static call graphs miss framework-
   driven control flow [63]. Runtime profiling or framework-specific analysis
   (Semgrep framework-native [63]) is more appropriate.
3. **Performance-critical profiling:** Use flamegraphs (py-spy), not call
   graphs. sys.settrace overhead (10x+) [59] invalidates timing data.
4. **Production monitoring:** Use sampling profilers [61]. Dynamic call graph
   tools (pycallgraph) are unsuitable for production [59].

## Gaps and Limitations

- No single tool covers all use cases. A typical workflow requires 2-3 tools.
- The "codebase comprehension" use case is poorly served by existing tools for
  codebases >2,000 nodes, where visualization becomes unreadable [57][58].
- No Python-specific tool provides interactive call graph exploration comparable
  to Sourcetrail (which is archived and had limited Python support).
- VizTracer is the closest to a general-purpose "see what happened" tool but
  focuses on profiling, not call graph construction.
